initial_observation.demographics: The patient was a young man in his 20s
initial_observation.encounter_context: The patient presented to a clinic and was later referred to a hospital for further evaluation after persistent fever and worsening back pain and rash
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The patient had chills 4 days prior, a headache, fever of 38.7℃, vomiting, negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR, and was prescribed cefditoren pivoxil without symptom improvement. He had pre-existing atopic dermatitis and lumbar disk hernia. A painless rash on the right occipital region was noted, and symptoms worsened despite antipyretic analgesics
presenting_symptoms: painless rash on the right side of the occipital region
known_prior_history: no history of varicella or shingles

evidence_items.source_text: On arrival, his vital signs were: Although his general appearance was sickly, he had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15, and his cognition was clear.

The patient had a painless rash on the right side of the occipital region (figure 1). Atopic dermatitis was also present on his back and lower legs. He exhibited no nuchal rigidity or jolt accentuation of the neck. Spontaneous back pain consistent with lumbar herniation was noted, but there was no spinal tapping pain. He was oriented to date, location and memory, and no unusual neurological abnormalities were observed.

Meningitis was suspected, and a lumbar puncture was performed immediately. The CSF was clear and colourless, with the following characteristics. Gram staining of centrifuged CSF revealed primarily mononuclear leucocytes, but no bacteria were detected (figure 2). Testing for serum HIV antigen and antibody was negative. Bacterial and mycobacterial cultures were obtained from the CSF, along with two sets of blood cultures. PCR testing for herpes simplex virus (HSV) was performed to assess the need for antiviral therapy. MRI revealed no abnormal intracranial signals.
The finding of lymphocyte predominance led to a diagnosis of aseptic meningitis; however, the 28 mg/dL glucose level was too low for a diagnosis of viral meningitis.
The CSF PCR test results for HSV were negative.

The residual volume of refrigerated CSF was used to perform VZV PCR, which detected VZV DNA at 11×106 copies/mL, confirming the diagnosis of viral meningitis caused by VZV. Serum VZV antibodies were positive for both IgM and IgG, confirming the reactivation of VZV infection.

The patient was then admitted to our hospital. Acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) and ampicillin (2 g every 6 hours) were administered intravenously. Ampicillin treatment was discontinued after blood and CSF cultures tested negative. After hospitalisation, the exudate from a painless skin rash on the right occipital area worsened. A dermatologist evaluated the patient and diagnosed herpes zoster based on the nature, distribution and associated pain of the rash.
The patient’s fever resolved and his symptoms improved. After 5 days of intravenous acyclovir treatment, the patient was discharged with 5 days of oral valacyclovir 1000 mg three times per day.

10 days later, the patient visited our clinic for follow-up. His right occipital rash persisted, but was crusted (figure 1). The patient was designated as fully recovered and was fully discharged from our service.
